=== [0:22] 안녕 ===
meaning: Hi.
tone: Informal, greeting.
--- word ---
term: 안녕
type: Interjection
breakdown: 
meaning: Hi / Hello / Bye
notes: 안녕 (annyeong) is the informal (반말, banmal) way to say both 'hello' and 'goodbye' to friends or people of the same age or younger. The formal equivalent for 'hello' is 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo).

=== [0:41] 감기가 심하게 들어서 ===
meaning: Because I caught a bad cold...
tone: Informal, explanatory, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: 감기가
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 감기 + 가
meaning: a cold (as the subject)
notes: 감기 (gamgi) means 'a common cold'. The particle 가 (ga) marks it as the subject of the sentence. It is used after nouns ending in a vowel. The alternative, 이 (i), is used after nouns ending in a consonant.
--- word ---
term: 심하게
type: Adverb
breakdown: 심하다 + -게
meaning: severely, badly
notes: The -게 (-ge) suffix is attached to the stem of a descriptive verb (adjective) to turn it into an adverb. 심하다 (simhada) means 'to be severe'.
--- word ---
term: 들어서
type: Verb
breakdown: 들다 + -어서
meaning: because (I) caught...
notes: While 감기에 걸리다 (gamgi-e geollida) is the most common phrase for 'to catch a cold', 감기가 들다 (gamgi-ga deulda) is also a natural expression. The -어서 (-eoseo) ending indicates the reason for the following clause.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V/A + -어서/아서
meaning: A connective ending that means 'because' or 'so', indicating that the first clause is the reason for the second clause.
example: 피곤해서 일찍 잤어요. (pigonhaeseo iljjik jasseoyo.) - I was tired, so I went to bed early.
level: Beginner

=== [0:43] 내 숨소리가 좀 시끄러울 거야 ===
meaning: My breathing will probably be a bit loud.
tone: Informal, apologetic, giving a heads-up.
--- word ---
term: 내
type: Pronoun
breakdown: 나 + 의
meaning: my
notes: 내 (nae) is the informal contraction of 나의 (na-ui), meaning 'my'. The formal equivalent is 제 (je), from 저의 (jeo-ui).
--- word ---
term: 숨소리가
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 숨소리 + 가
meaning: the sound of breathing
notes: 숨소리 (sumsori) is a compound noun from 숨 (sum, 'breath') and 소리 (sori, 'sound'). The particle 가 (ga) marks it as the subject.
--- word ---
term: 좀
type: Adverb
breakdown: Contraction of 조금
meaning: a bit, a little
notes: 좀 (jom) is a very common colloquial contraction of 조금 (jogeum). It can mean 'a bit' or be used to soften a request, making it sound more polite or less demanding.
--- word ---
term: 시끄러울 거야
type: Adjective + Ending
breakdown: 시끄럽다 + -을 거야
meaning: will probably be loud
notes: The -(으)ㄹ 거야 (-eul geoya) ending is the informal (반말, banmal) future tense. It can express an intention or, as in this case, a supposition or guess about a future state. The formal equivalent is -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-eul geoyeyo).
--- grammar ---
pattern: A/V + -(으)ㄹ 거야
meaning: An informal future tense ending used to express an intention, plan, or supposition. Used with friends and people younger than you.
example: 주말에 영화 볼 거야. (jumal-e yeonghwa bol geoya.) - I'm going to watch a movie on the weekend.
level: Beginner

=== [1:02] 근데 이렇게 콧물 맛이 ===
meaning: But the taste of snot like this...
tone: Informal, descriptive, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: 근데
type: Conjunction
breakdown: Contraction of 그런데
meaning: But / By the way
notes: 근데 (geunde) is a very common spoken contraction of 그런데 (geureonde). It can show contrast ('but') or be used to change the subject ('by the way').
--- word ---
term: 이렇게
type: Adverb
breakdown: 이렇다 + -게
meaning: like this, in this way
notes: This is part of a set: 이렇게 (ireoke, like this), 그렇게 (geureoke, like that), 저렇게 (jeoreoke, like that over there). It describes how an action is done.
--- word ---
term: 콧물
type: Noun
breakdown: 코 + 물
meaning: snot, runny nose
notes: A compound noun literally meaning 'nose water'. It's the standard term for a runny nose or snot.
--- word ---
term: 맛이
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 맛 + 이
meaning: the taste (as the subject)
notes: The subject particle 이 (i) is used because the noun 맛 (mat) ends in a consonant. The sentence trails off, leaving the predicate unsaid.

=== [1:10] 너무 TMI였다 ===
meaning: That was too much TMI.
tone: Informal, self-aware, humorous.
--- word ---
term: 너무
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: too, very
notes: While traditionally meaning 'too (much)' in a negative sense, in modern colloquial Korean, 너무 (neomu) is frequently used to mean 'very' or 'really' in both positive and negative contexts (e.g., 너무 좋아 - neomu joa, 'I like it so much').
--- word ---
term: TMI였다
type: Loanword + Verb
breakdown: TMI + -이었다
meaning: was TMI
notes: TMI (Too Much Information) is a common English acronym used in casual Korean. It's combined with -이었다 (-ieotda), the plain form past tense of the copula 이다 (ida, 'to be'), used after a noun ending in a consonant.

=== [1:11] 자 이건 취소 ===
meaning: Okay, I take that back.
tone: Informal, playful, corrective.
--- word ---
term: 자
type: Interjection
breakdown: 
meaning: Okay, Alright, Now
notes: 자 (ja) is a filler word used to get attention, transition to a new topic, or encourage action, similar to 'Alright, then...' or 'Okay, now...' in English.
--- word ---
term: 이건
type: Pronoun + Particle
breakdown: 이것 + 은
meaning: this (as for this)
notes: 이건 (igeon) is a common contraction of 이것은 (igeos-eun). 이것 (igeot) means 'this thing', and 은 (eun) is the topic marking particle, indicating that 'this' (her previous TMI comment) is the topic of discussion.
--- word ---
term: 취소
type: Noun
breakdown: 
meaning: cancellation
notes: Using just the noun 취소 (chwiso) at the end of a sentence is a very casual and abbreviated way of saying 'I cancel it' or 'It's cancelled'. The full sentence might be 이건 취소야 (igeon chwisoya).

=== [1:20] 감기 유행이래? ===
meaning: Is the flu going around?
tone: Informal, questioning, likely reacting to a fan's comment.
--- word ---
term: 감기
type: Noun
breakdown: 
meaning: cold, flu
notes: Refers to the common cold or flu.
--- word ---
term: 유행이래?
type: Noun + Verb Ending
breakdown: 유행 + 이다 + -래?
meaning: (Do they say) it's a trend?
notes: 유행 (yuhaeng) means 'trend' or 'fashion'. The ending -래? (-rae?) is a casual contraction of -라고 해? (-rago hae?), used to ask for confirmation of something one has heard. It implies she is reacting to information she just received, likely from a fan's comment.
--- grammar ---
pattern: Noun + -(이)래?
meaning: An informal quoted speech question ending. It's used to ask about something you heard from someone else, meaning 'Is it true that...?' or 'Did you/they say that...?'.
example: 오늘 시험이래? (oneul siheom-irae?) - Did they say the exam is today?
level: Intermediate

=== [1:22] 역시 트렌드세터야 ===
meaning: As expected, I'm a trendsetter.
tone: Informal, joking, sarcastic.
--- word ---
term: 역시
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: as expected, indeed
notes: 역시 (yeoksi) is used when a result confirms a prior thought or expectation. It's a very common conversational adverb. A slangy, shortened version is 옄싀 (yeokswi).
--- word ---
term: 트렌드세터야
type: Loanword + Verb
breakdown: 트렌드세터 + -이야
meaning: (I) am a trendsetter
notes: 트렌드세터 (teurendeuseteo) is a loanword from 'trendsetter'. It's combined with -이야 (-iya), the informal (반말, banmal) ending for the verb 이다 (ida, 'to be') used after a noun ending in a vowel. The subject 'I' (나, na) is omitted, which is typical in Korean when the context is clear.

=== [1:24] 오케이 좋았어 ===
meaning: Okay, that was good.
tone: Informal, affirmative, self-directed.
--- word ---
term: 오케이
type: Interjection / Loanword
breakdown: 
meaning: Okay
notes: A direct loanword from the English word 'Okay,' commonly used in casual Korean conversation to express agreement or transition to a new thought.
--- word ---
term: 좋았어
type: Adjective
breakdown: 좋다 + -았- + -어
meaning: was good
notes: The past tense, informal (반말, banmal) form of 좋다 (to be good). The -았- infix indicates past tense, and the -어 ending is the informal, non-polite ending. It can be used to describe a past state or action, like 'It was good' or 'That went well.'

=== [1:34] 아 걱정돼 ===
meaning: Ah, I'm worried.
tone: Informal, expressing concern.
--- word ---
term: 아
type: Interjection
breakdown: 
meaning: Ah / Oh
notes: A common interjection used to express a wide range of emotions like surprise, realization, pain, or, as in this case, a sudden feeling or thought.
--- word ---
term: 걱정돼
type: Verb
breakdown: 걱정되다
meaning: to be worried
notes: The informal present tense form of 걱정되다 (to become worried). It's a contraction of 걱정되어. This passive form implies that the state of worry is happening to the speaker, as opposed to the active verb 걱정하다 (to worry), which describes the action of worrying.

=== [1:39] 내일 괜찮을까 ===
meaning: Will I be okay tomorrow?
tone: Informal, questioning, expressing doubt to oneself.
--- word ---
term: 내일
type: Noun / Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: tomorrow
notes: Can function as a noun ('Tomorrow is my birthday') or an adverb ('I'll go tomorrow'), as it does here. No particle is needed when used adverbially.
--- word ---
term: 괜찮을까
type: Adjective
breakdown: 괜찮다 + -(으)ㄹ까
meaning: will it be okay? / I wonder if it will be okay
notes: Combines the adjective 괜찮다 (to be okay) with the -(으)ㄹ까 ending. This ending is used to express doubt, wonder, or to ask a question to oneself. It often translates to 'I wonder if...' or 'Do you think...?'
--- grammar ---
pattern: V/A + -(으)ㄹ까(요)?
meaning: Used to express wonder, ask a question to oneself ('I wonder if...'), or make a suggestion to others ('Shall we...?').
example: 우리 영화 볼까? (Shall we watch a movie?)
level: Beginner

=== [1:48] 밖에서 안 먹고 ===
meaning: (I) didn't eat outside and...
tone: Informal, explanatory, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: 밖에서
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 밖 + -에서
meaning: outside
notes: 밖 means 'outside.' The particle -에서 indicates the location where an action takes place. It's often contrasted with 안에서 (inside).
--- word ---
term: 안
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: not
notes: A short-form negator placed directly before a verb or adjective. It's more common in spoken Korean than the long-form negation using -지 않다. For example, 안 먹다 is the same as 먹지 않다 (to not eat).
--- word ---
term: 먹고
type: Verb
breakdown: 먹다 + -고
meaning: eat and...
notes: The verb stem 먹다 (to eat) is combined with the connecting particle -고. -고 is used to link two clauses, often in sequential order ('I did A and then did B') or to simply list actions. The sentence is incomplete, implying the next action will follow.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V + -고
meaning: A connective ending that links two clauses. It can mean 'and,' 'and then,' or show a simple sequence of actions.
example: 밥을 먹고 영화를 봤어요. (I ate and then watched a movie.)
level: Beginner

=== [1:50] 집에서 먹었어 ===
meaning: I ate at home.
tone: Informal, explanatory, completing the previous thought.
--- word ---
term: 집에서
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 집 + -에서
meaning: at home
notes: 집 means 'home.' The particle -에서 marks the location where an action (먹었어, ate) occurs. A common mistake for learners is using -에. Use -에 for a static location (집에 있어요 - I am at home) and -에서 for an action's location (집에서 공부해요 - I study at home).
--- word ---
term: 먹었어
type: Verb
breakdown: 먹다 + -었- + -어
meaning: ate
notes: The past tense, informal (반말, banmal) form of 먹다 (to eat). The -었- infix indicates past tense, and the -어 ending is the informal, non-polite ending.

=== [1:53] 너무 많이 먹었나 봐 ===
meaning: I guess I ate too much.
tone: Informal, speculative, self-reflective.
--- word ---
term: 너무
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: too / very
notes: Traditionally, 너무 meant 'too' in a negative sense (e.g., 너무 비싸요 - It's too expensive). However, in modern colloquial Korean, it's very common to use it to mean 'very' or 'really' in a positive sense as well (e.g., 너무 좋아요 - It's really good).
--- word ---
term: 많이
type: Adverb
breakdown: 많다 + -이
meaning: a lot / much
notes: The adverbial form of the adjective 많다 (to be many/much). The -이 suffix is one way to turn an adjective stem into an adverb.
--- word ---
term: 먹었나
type: Verb
breakdown: 먹다 + -었- + -나
meaning: I guess I ate
notes: This is part of the -나 보다 grammar pattern. It combines the past tense stem of 먹다 (먹었-) with -나, which is used to express a guess or assumption.
--- word ---
term: 봐
type: Verb
breakdown: 보다
meaning: it seems
notes: The informal form of 보다 (to see), but in the pattern -나 보다, it loses its literal meaning and functions as a grammatical ending to mean 'it seems like' or 'I guess that'.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V/A + -(으)ㄴ/나 보다
meaning: Expresses a guess, assumption, or supposition based on some evidence or observation. It translates to 'it seems like...' or 'I guess that...'. For past tense, -았/었나 보다 is used.
example: 그 사람이 바빴나 봐요. (I guess that person was busy.)
level: Intermediate

=== [2:01] 그 와중에 매니저님이 사다 주셨나? ===
meaning: In the midst of all that, did my manager buy it for me?
tone: Informal, questioning, trying to recall a memory.
--- word ---
term: 그
type: Determiner
breakdown: 
meaning: that
notes: A determiner used to refer to something previously mentioned or understood from context. Here, it refers to the general situation of her being sick.
--- word ---
term: 와중에
type: Noun phrase
breakdown: 와중 + -에
meaning: in the midst of / meanwhile
notes: The phrase 그 와중에 means 'in the middle of that situation' or 'despite all that.' It's used to highlight that something happened while another, often more significant, event was ongoing.
--- word ---
term: 매니저님이
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 매니저 + -님 + -이
meaning: the manager (subject)
notes: 매니저 is 'manager.' -님 is an honorific suffix showing respect. -이 is the subject-marking particle. Using -님 indicates a formal, respectful relationship with her manager.
--- word ---
term: 사다
type: Verb
breakdown: 사(서) + 주다
meaning: to buy and give
notes: This is the stem of the compound verb 사다 주다. It combines 사다 (to buy) and 주다 (to give), meaning 'to buy something for someone.' The full verb here is 사다 주셨나?.
--- word ---
term: 주셨나?
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 주다 + -시- + -었- + -나?
meaning: did (someone respected) give?
notes: A complex ending. 주다 (to give) + -시- (honorific for the manager) + -었- (past tense) + -나? (informal question ending expressing self-doubt or wonder). The full verb is 사다 주셨나? (Did they buy it for me?).
--- grammar ---
pattern: V + -아/어 주다
meaning: Indicates that an action is performed for someone's benefit. It means 'to do [verb] for someone.'
example: 문을 열어 주세요. (Please open the door for me.)
level: Beginner
--- grammar ---
pattern: -시- (Honorific Infix)
meaning: An infix added to verb/adjective stems to show respect for the subject of the sentence. It is used here because the subject is 매니저님 (manager).
example: 선생님께서 오셨어요. (The teacher came.)
level: Beginner

=== [2:06] 또 웃긴 거 ===
meaning: Another funny thing...
tone: Informal, transitional. Introducing a new anecdote.
--- word ---
term: 또
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: again, also, another
notes: 또 (tto) can mean 'again' (repetition of an action) or 'also/in addition' (adding a new piece of information). Here, it's used to add another story, like saying 'And another thing...'
--- word ---
term: 웃긴
type: Adjective
breakdown: 웃기다 + -ㄴ
meaning: funny
notes: This is the descriptive form of the verb 웃기다 (utgida), meaning 'to be funny.' The -ㄴ ending modifies the following noun, 거 (geo), turning the phrase into 'a funny thing'.
--- word ---
term: 거
type: Noun (pronoun)
breakdown: 것
meaning: thing
notes: 거 (geo) is the colloquial contraction of 것 (geot), which means 'thing' or 'stuff'. In spoken Korean, 거 is used far more frequently than the full form 것.
--- grammar ---
pattern: Adjective + -(으)ㄴ + Noun
meaning: This is the standard way to use an adjective to describe a noun. The adjective stem is followed by -ㄴ (if it ends in a vowel) or -은 (if it ends in a consonant).
example: 예쁘다 (to be pretty) -> 예쁜 사람 (a pretty person)
level: Beginner

=== [2:08] 아픈 와중에 또 ===
meaning: While I was sick, again...
tone: Informal, narrative. Setting the scene for her story.
--- word ---
term: 아픈
type: Adjective
breakdown: 아프다 + -ㄴ
meaning: sick, painful
notes: The descriptive form of 아프다 (apeuda), 'to be sick/hurt'. Here it modifies 와중 (wajung), meaning 'the midst of being sick'.
--- word ---
term: 와중에
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 와중 + -에
meaning: in the midst of, while
notes: The pattern '-(으)ㄴ/는 와중에' means 'while (something) was happening' or 'in the midst of...'. It often implies that the second action happened despite the first situation (being sick).
--- word ---
term: 또
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: again, also
notes: Here, 또 (tto) connects back to the previous sentence, continuing the thought and adding another element to her story.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -(으)ㄴ/는 와중에
meaning: Indicates that an action takes place 'in the midst of' or 'during' another ongoing situation. It emphasizes that something happened despite the circumstances.
example: 바쁜 와중에 와 주셔서 감사합니다. (Thank you for coming despite being busy.)
level: Intermediate

=== [2:10] 홍콩 와플을 먹고 왔어 ===
meaning: I went and ate a Hong Kong waffle.
tone: Informal, narrative. Stating the main point of her anecdote.
--- word ---

type: Noun

notes: A proper noun for Hong Kong.

type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 와플 + -을

breakdown: 오다 + -았어
meaning: came

pattern: Verb Stem + -고 오다/가다
meaning: Means 'to go/come and do something'. It implies doing an action at another location and then returning or arriving. 먹고 왔어 literally means 'I ate and came back', implying she went out to eat.
example: 친구 만나고 왔어요. (I met a friend and came back.)
level: Beginner

=== [2:27] 와플 어디였더라 이름이 ===
meaning: The waffle place... what was its name again?
tone: Informal, self-questioning, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: 와플
type: Noun
breakdown: 
meaning: waffle
notes: In this context, 'waffle' is used as shorthand for 'the waffle shop'.
--- word ---
term: 어디였더라
type: Interrogative + Verb Ending
breakdown: 어디 + -이다 + -었더라
meaning: where was it again?
notes: The sentence word order is inverted for a natural, spoken feel. The standard order would be '이름이 어디였더라?'. The -더라 ending is used when recalling something from personal experience.
--- word ---
term: 이름이
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 이름 + -이
meaning: the name (is)
notes: 이름 (ireum) means 'name'. The particle -이 (i) marks it as the subject of the sentence.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -더라
meaning: A retrospective sentence ending used when the speaker is recalling something they personally saw, heard, or felt. It often carries a nuance of mild surprise or self-questioning, as if thinking out loud.
example: 그 영화 정말 재미있더라. (I recall that movie was really fun.)
level: Intermediate

=== [2:31] M이 들어갔는데 ===
meaning: It had an 'M' in it, but...
tone: Informal, trying to recall, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: M이
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: M + -이
meaning: 'M' (as subject)
notes: The subject particle -이 (i) is attached directly to the English letter 'M', treating it as a noun.
--- word ---
term: 들어갔는데
type: Verb
breakdown: 들어가다 + -았는데
meaning: it was in it, but...
notes: 들어가다 (deureogada) means 'to go in' or 'to be included'. The -는데 (neunde) ending here provides background information and trails off, implying she still can't remember the full name.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -(으)ㄴ/는데
meaning: A versatile connective ending. It can provide background context ('...and...'), show contrast ('...but...'), or be used at the end of a sentence to trail off, leaving the thought unfinished.
example: 지금 밖에 비 오는데... (It's raining outside right now, so...)
level: Beginner

=== [2:41] 와플을 너무 많이 먹어서 ===
meaning: Because I ate too many waffles...
tone: Informal, explanatory. Giving a reason for the next statement.
--- word ---
term: 와플을
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 와플 + -을
meaning: waffles (as object)
notes: The particle -을 (eul) marks 'waffle' as the direct object of the verb 먹다 (meokda).
--- word ---
term: 너무
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: too, very
notes: While traditionally meaning 'too' (implying excess), in modern colloquial Korean, 너무 (neomu) is frequently used to mean 'very' or 'really' in both positive and negative contexts. E.g., 너무 좋아요 (It's so good).
--- word ---
term: 많이
type: Adverb
breakdown: 많다 + -이
meaning: a lot, many
notes: 많이 (mani) is the adverbial form of the adjective 많다 (manta), meaning 'to be many/much'.
--- word ---
term: 먹어서
type: Verb
breakdown: 먹다 + -어서
meaning: because I ate
notes: The -아/어서 (aseo/eoseo) ending indicates a cause-and-effect relationship. 'Because I did X, Y happened.' This clause provides the reason for the action in the next sentence.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -아/어서
meaning: A connective ending used to show a logical reason or cause for the following clause. The action in the first clause must happen before the action in the second.
example: 피곤해서 일찍 잤어요. (I was tired, so I went to bed early.)
level: Beginner

--- grammar ---
pattern: -거든(요)
meaning: A sentence ending used to provide a reason or explanation for something already said or about to be said. It has a casual, conversational feel and implies the listener may not be aware of this information.
example: 왜 늦었어요? - 길이 많이 막혔거든요. (Why were you late? - Because the traffic was really bad, you see.)

notes: The informal question form of 좋다. Be careful not to confuse 좋다 (to be good, adjective) with 좋아하다 (to like, verb). '감기약이 좋아' (The cold medicine is good) vs. '감기약을 좋아해' (I like the cold medicine).

meaning: cold medicine

--- word ---

meaning: among...
notes: 중 means 'among' or 'in the middle of'. The particle -에서는 is a combination of -에서 ('in'/'at') and -는 (topic marker), adding emphasis or contrast. It means something like 'specifically among these options...'
--- grammar ---
pattern: V-어/아 보다
meaning: Expresses trying or experiencing something.

--- grammar ---
pattern: Past Tense Adjective Form (-ㄴ/은)
meaning: Turns a verb or adjective into a modifier for a noun, describing a past action or state.

=== [13:54] 그렇게 밝게 ===

--- grammar ---
pattern: 못 + Verb
meaning: Indicates the inability to perform an action due to external factors or lack of skill. Used with action verbs.

=== [22:30] 가끔씩은 예쁘긴 한데 ===
meaning: Sometimes it does look pretty, but...
tone: Informal, concessive, trailing off.
--- word ---
term: 가끔씩은
type: Adverb + particle
breakdown: 가끔씩 (sometimes) + -은 (topic/contrast particle)
meaning: at least sometimes
notes: 가끔 and 가끔씩 both mean 'sometimes'. The particle -은 adds a nuance of contrast: 'At least at *some* times (it's pretty, but at other times it's not).'
--- word ---
term: 예쁘긴
type: Adjective + particle
breakdown: 예쁘다 (to be pretty) + -기는 (concessive particle)
meaning: is pretty, but...
notes: This is a contraction of 예쁘기는. The '-기는 하다' pattern is used to acknowledge a fact while intending to contrast it with another point. It translates to 'It is indeed..., but...' or 'I admit it's..., but...'
--- word ---
term: 한데
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 하다 (to do/be) + -ㄴ데 (background/contrast ending)
meaning: it is, but...
notes: This completes the '-기는 하다' pattern. The -ㄴ데 ending provides the contrast, leading into an unstated 'but...'. The full pattern is A/V-기는 한데.
--- grammar ---
pattern: A/V-기는 하다 / A/V-긴 하다
meaning: Used to acknowledge or admit a point, before usually presenting a contrasting idea. 'It is true that... but...', 'I admit that... but...'.
example: 비싸긴 한데 정말 맛있어. (It is expensive, I admit, but it's really delicious.)

notes: This is part of the present progressive 'V-고 있다' pattern. '뭐' (what) combines with '하다' (to do). The '-고' is a connective ending.
--- word ---
term: 있는데
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 있다 + -는데
meaning: are...
notes: A common sentence ending used to provide background context before asking a question, making a suggestion, or presenting a contrasting idea. It makes the question sound softer and more conversational than a direct '뭐하고 있어?'.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V-고 있다
meaning: Indicates a continuous action, equivalent to the English present progressive ('be + V-ing').
example: 지금 밥 먹고 있어요. (I'm eating right now.)
level: Beginner

breakdown: 
meaning: not
notes: This is the short-form negator in Korean. It is placed directly before a verb or adjective. The long-form negation is 'V-지 않다' (e.g., '하지 않으면'). The short form is more common in conversation.
--- word ---
term: 하고
type: verb
breakdown: 하다 + -고
meaning: do and...
notes: The '-고' (go) ending connects two clauses sequentially. Here, it connects '안 하다' (not do) and '자다' (sleep), meaning 'not doing it and then sleeping'.
--- word ---
term: 자면
type: verb
breakdown: 자다 + -면
meaning: if (I) sleep
notes: The '-(으)면' (-(eu)myeon) ending attaches to a verb or adjective stem to create a conditional clause, meaning 'if' or 'when'.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V-지 않고 / 안 V-고
meaning: Expresses 'without doing V'. It indicates that the action in the first clause is not performed, and then the action in the second clause is. Here, '안 하고 자면' means 'if I sleep without doing it'.
example: 아침을 안 먹고 학교에 갔어요. (I went to school without eating breakfast.)

notes: The '-(으)ㄹ' ending turns the adjective '좋다' into a modifier that describes a future or potential state for the following noun, '때' (time).
--- word ---
term: 땐
type: Noun + particle (contraction)
breakdown: 때 (time/when) + -는 (topic particle)
meaning: as for when
notes: A common contraction in spoken Korean. '때' means 'time' or 'when'. The pattern '-(으)ㄹ 때' means 'when [verb/adjective]'. The topic particle '-는' emphasizes this specific time.
--- word ---
term: 쉬는
type: Verb
breakdown: 쉬다 + -는
meaning: resting
notes: The '-는' ending turns the verb '쉬다' (to rest) into a modifier that describes the following noun, '게' (thing/act).
--- word ---
term: 게
type: Noun (contraction)
breakdown: 것 (thing) + -이 (subject particle)
meaning: the act of
notes: '-는 것' is a grammar pattern called a nominalizer; it turns a verb phrase ('쉬다') into a noun phrase ('쉬는 것' - the act of resting). '게' is the very common spoken contraction of '것이'.
--- word ---
term: 좋대
type: Adjective + ending (contraction)
breakdown: 좋다 + -다고 해
meaning: they say it's good
notes: '-대' is a colloquial contraction of the quoted speech pattern '-다고 해'. It's used to report something you heard from someone else or general knowledge. It's very common in casual conversation.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -대(요)
meaning: A colloquial quoted speech ending, short for '-다고 해(요)'. Used to report something one has heard. Means 'they say...' or 'I heard that...'.
example: 이 식당이 맛있대. (They say this restaurant is delicious.)

term: 좀
type: Adverb
breakdown: 조금 (contraction)
meaning: a little, a bit
notes: 좀 is a very common contraction of 조금 (jogeum), both meaning 'a little'. In spoken Korean, 좀 is used far more frequently due to its ease of pronunciation. It can also be used to soften a request, making it sound more polite, e.g., '물 좀 주세요' (mul jom juseyo) - 'Please give me some water.'
--- word ---
term: 더
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: more
notes: 더 is placed before a verb or adjective to mean 'more'. For example, '더 주세요' (deo juseyo) means 'Please give me more,' and '더 빨라요' (deo ppallayo) means 'It's faster.'
--- word ---
term: 하고 싶다
type: Verb phrase
breakdown: 하다 + -고 싶다
meaning: to want to do
notes: The '-고 싶다' (-go sipda) pattern attaches to a verb stem to express the speaker's desire or wish to do that action. It's a fundamental pattern for expressing wants. The speaker is using the informal, non-conjugated dictionary form here, which is common in casual, self-directed speech.
--- word ---
term: 하면
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 하다 + -(으)면
meaning: if (I) do
notes: -(으)면 is a connective ending that means 'if' or 'when'. It's attached to verb or adjective stems. If the stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ, -면 is used (e.g., 가면 - if I go). If it ends in a consonant (except ㄹ), -으면 is used (e.g., 먹으면 - if I eat).
--- word ---
term: 40분
type: Noun
breakdown: 40 + 분
meaning: 40 minutes
notes: 분 (bun) is the native Korean counter for minutes. It's used with Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼...). For example, '10분' (sip-bun) is '10 minutes'.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V-고 싶다
meaning: Expresses the speaker's desire to do something; 'to want to (verb)'.
example: 영화를 보고 싶어요. (I want to watch a movie.)
level: Beginner
--- grammar ---
pattern: V/A-(으)면
meaning: A conditional clause meaning 'if' or 'when'.
example: 비가 오면 집에 있을 거예요. (If it rains, I'm going to stay home.)

breakdown: 하다 + -아/어 오다 + -았/었었- + -거든
meaning: I had been doing it, you see.
notes: This form is packed with meaning. 해오다 (haeda + oda) means 'to have been doing something up to now'. The double past tense -았었- (asseot) emphasizes a past action that is now finished. --- grammar ---
pattern: -았/었었- (Double Past Tense)
meaning: Indicates an action that happened and was completed in the more distant past, and is no longer relevant to the present. It emphasizes the disconnect from the present more strongly than the simple past tense -았/었-.
example: 어렸을 때 미국에 갔었어요. (I went to America when I was young [and am not there now].)
level: Intermediate
--- grammar ---
pattern: -거든(요)
meaning: A sentence ending used in conversation to provide a reason, explanation, or background for a previous statement. It implies '...you see,' or 'it's because...'. It's used when giving new information.
example: 어제 못 갔어요. 너무 피곤했거든요. (I couldn't go yesterday. I was so tired, you see.)

notes: 내 is the informal pronoun for 'my,' a contraction of 나의 (na-ui). In spoken Korean, this contracted form is almost always used. The formal equivalent is 제 (je), from 저의 (jeo-ui).
--- word ---
term: 처음
type: Noun/Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: first
notes: Can mean 'the first time' as a noun or 'for the first time' as an adverb. Here it functions like an adjective modifying 운동화 (sneakers) to mean 'first sneakers'.
--- word ---
term: 그
type: Determiner
breakdown: 
meaning: that/those
notes: 그 refers to something previously mentioned or known to the listener but not currently present. It contrasts with 이 (this, near speaker) and 저 (that, far from both).
--- word ---
term: 운동화는
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 운동화 (sneakers) + -는 (topic particle)
meaning: as for the sneakers
notes: The topic particle -는 sets 'sneakers' as the main subject of the sentence, often to contrast it with something else (in this case, her new shoes).

=== [34:15] 뛰고 나서 항상 다리가 좀 피로하고 ===
meaning: after running, my legs were always a bit tired and...
tone: Informal, descriptive, listing past conditions.
--- word ---
term: 뛰고 나서
type: Verb phrase
breakdown: 뛰다 (to run) + -고 나서 (after doing)
meaning: after running
notes: A common conversational pattern to show a sequence of actions. It's similar to V-(으)ㄴ 후에 but often feels more immediate and spoken.
--- word ---
term: 항상
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: always
notes: A common adverb of frequency. It is often interchangeable with the native Korean word 늘 (neul).
--- word ---
term: 다리가
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 다리 (leg) + -가 (subject particle)
meaning: legs (as the subject)
notes: The subject marking particle -가 identifies 'legs' as the subject of the verb 피로하다 (to be tired).
--- word ---
term: 좀
type: Adverb
breakdown: 조금 -> 좀
meaning: a bit, a little
notes: 좀 is a very common contraction of 조금. It's used here to soften the statement, implying 'a little bit' tired rather than 'extremely' tired.
--- word ---
term: 피로하고
type: Verb (connective form)
breakdown: 피로하다 (to be fatigued) + -고 (and)
meaning: be tired and...
notes: 피로하다 is often used for physical fatigue or exhaustion from exertion, whereas 피곤하다 (pigonhada) is more general tiredness (e.g., from lack of sleep). The -고 ending connects this clause to the next one about her ankles.

=== [34:18] 발목도 피로하고 이랬었단 말이야 ===
meaning: my ankles were tired too, you know.
tone: Informal, explanatory, emphatic.
--- word ---
term: 발목도
type: Noun + Particle
breakdown: 발목 (ankle) + -도 (also/too)
meaning: ankles too
notes: 발목 is a compound noun: 발 (foot) + 목 (neck). The particle -도 adds the meaning of 'also' or 'in addition to'.
--- word ---
term: 피로하고
type: Verb (connective form)
breakdown: 피로하다 (to be fatigued) + -고 (and)
meaning: be tired and...
notes: This verb repeats from the previous clause, linking the two symptoms of fatigue.
--- word ---
term: 이랬었단
type: Verb phrase (contracted)
breakdown: 이렇다 (to be like this) -> 이랬었다 (double past) + -는 -> -단
meaning: that it used to be like this
notes: This is a complex contraction. 이랬었다 is the 'double past' tense (-았/었었-), emphasizing a state that was true in the past but is no longer. The full form is 이랬었다는, which is contracted to 이랬었단.
--- word ---
term: 말이야
type: Noun + Copula
breakdown: 말 (word/speech) + -이야 (is, informal)
meaning: I'm saying...
notes: The full phrase -(ㄴ/는)단 말이야 is a common colloquial ending used to emphasize a statement or provide an explanation, similar to adding "you see" or "I'm telling you" in English.
--- grammar ---
pattern: -았/었었다 (Double Past Tense)
meaning: Indicates a past action or state that was completed and is now disconnected from the present. It often implies a change in state and can be translated as 'used to be...' or 'had been...'.
example: 저는 어렸을 때 키가 작았었어요. (I used to be short when I was young.)
level: Intermediate
--- grammar ---
pattern: -(ㄴ/는)단 말이야
meaning: A colloquial sentence ender used to emphasize a statement, provide an explanation, or express mild frustration. It's like saying 'I'm telling you...' or '...you see.'
example: 이게 더 좋단 말이야. (I'm telling you, this one is better.)
level: Intermediate

breakdown: 그런데 -> 근데

=== [34:24] 진짜 ===
meaning: Really.
tone: Emphatic, informal.
--- word ---
term: 진짜
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: Really, truly
notes: A very common word in spoken Korean used to add emphasis, similar to 'really' or 'seriously'. It can function as an adverb modifying a verb/adjective (e.g., 진짜 예쁘다 - really pretty) or as a standalone interjection (e.g., 진짜? - Really?). === [34:25] 러닝화 제대로 된 걸 딱 신으니까 ===
meaning: As soon as I put on a proper pair of running shoes,
tone: Explanatory, informal, setting up a realization.
--- word ---
term: 러닝화
type: Noun
breakdown: 러닝 (running) + 화 (shoes)
meaning: Running shoes
notes: This is an example of Konglish (Korean-style English), combining the English word 'running' (러닝) with the Sino-Korean character '화' (靴), which means shoes or boots. Other examples include 운동화 (undonghwa - sneakers/exercise shoes) and 구두 (gudu - dress shoes, from Japanese 'kutsu').
--- word ---
term: 제대로
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: Properly, correctly, in the right way
notes: This adverb is used to express that an action is done thoroughly or correctly, not half-heartedly. For example, '밥 제대로 먹어' (bap jedaero meogeo) means 'Eat a proper meal'.
--- word ---
term: 된
type: Verb (adjective form)
breakdown: 되다 + -(으)ㄴ
meaning: that is/became
notes: This is the past tense adjectival form of the verb 되다 (doeda - to become). The -(으)ㄴ ending turns a verb into an adjective that can modify a noun. Here, '제대로 된' modifies '걸' (the thing), creating the meaning 'a thing that is proper'.
--- word ---
term: 걸
type: Noun + Particle (contraction)
breakdown: 것 + 을
meaning: the thing (as an object)
notes: 걸 is a very common contraction of 것을 (geoseul), where 것 (geot) means 'thing' or 'the one' and -을 (eul) is the object particle. In casual speech, contractions like this are the norm.
--- word ---
term: 딱
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: Exactly, perfectly, just right
notes: 딱 is a mimetic adverb that adds a sense of precision, suddenness, or firmness. Here, it emphasizes that the action of putting on the shoes was done perfectly and at the right moment, leading to a realization. It can also mean 'just' (e.g., 딱 하나 - just one).
--- word ---
term: 신으니까
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 신다 + -(으)니까
meaning: because I put them on / since I put them on
notes: The grammar pattern -(으)니까 indicates a reason or cause for the following clause. It's often used when the speaker is explaining a personal discovery or experience that led to a certain conclusion or feeling. It differs from -아/어서 (aseo/eoseo) in that it can be followed by commands or suggestions.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V + -(으)니까
meaning: Indicates the first clause is the reason or basis for the second clause, often based on the speaker's personal experience or discovery.
example: 밖에 비가 오니까 우산 가져가세요. (Bakke biga onikka usan gajyeogaseyo.) - It's raining outside, so take an umbrella.
level: Beginner

=== [34:30] 이래서 ===
meaning: This is why...
tone: Exclamatory, informal, expressing a realization.
--- word ---
term: 이래서
type: Adverbial phrase (contraction)
breakdown: 이러하다 + -아서
meaning: For this reason, this is why
notes: A contraction of 이러해서 (ireohaeseo), meaning 'because it is like this'. It's used to introduce a conclusion based on a reason that was just stated or is commonly understood. It's the spoken form of '이러므로' (ireomeuro). Compare with 그래서 (geuraeseo - so/therefore), which is more of a general connector.

=== [34:32] 이러는구나 했지 ===
meaning: I thought, 'Ah, so that's how it is.'
tone: Reflective, informal, describing a past realization.
--- word ---
term: 이러는구나
type: Verb ending (quoted thought)
breakdown: 이렇다 + -는구나
meaning: Oh, it's like this!
notes: The ending -는구나 (neunguna) is used to express a new realization or a mild sense of surprise upon learning something. It's a monologue-style exclamation. Here, it's part of an indirect quotation representing the speaker's thought.
--- word ---
term: 했지
type: Verb ending
breakdown: 하다 + -었- + -지
meaning: I did/thought
notes: This is a casual, retrospective use of 하다 (hada - to do/say/think). The -지 (ji) ending here implies a recollection or a statement of a past event as a fact, almost as if talking to oneself. The full structure is an implied quotation: "이러는구나"라고 했지 ('ireoneunguna'-rago haetji) - I thought, "So that's how it is."
--- grammar ---
pattern: V/A + -는구나/-구나
meaning: An exclamatory ending used when the speaker realizes or notices something for the first time. -는구나 is for verbs and 있다/없다, while -구나 is for adjectives.
example: 아, 저 사람이 배우구나! (A, jeo sarami baeuguna!) - Ah, so that person is an actor!
level: Intermediate

meaning: Expresses obligation or necessity, equivalent to 'must' or 'have to' in English.

notes: This common phrase literally means 'by knowing'. It implies taking care of something using one's own judgment and initiative, without needing to be told what to do. It conveys a sense of capability and autonomy.

meaning: because we'll beat (them)
notes: 패다 means 'to beat' or 'to hit'. This is strong, slangy language used playfully to mean 'we'll deal with them'. The '~(으)니까' ending indicates the reason for the following command ('don't worry').

--- word ---

meaning: don't
notes: The informal negative command ending. It attaches to a verb stem to tell someone not to do something. The full form is '~지 마라', but '~지 마' is standard in casual speech.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V + ~(으)니까
meaning: Indicates the reason for the following suggestion, command, or statement. Often translated as 'because' or 'so'.

--- grammar ---

--- grammar ---

meaning: A pattern used to nominalize a definition or a statement. It means 'the fact that...', 'the thing that is...', or 'the thing called...'.

notes: Literally means 'material' or 'quality'. In modern slang, it's used to mean 'vibe', 'type', or 'material' (as in 'boyfriend material'). 'X 재질' means 'has the vibe of X'.

=== [56:57] 아니야 내가 먹었다는 게 아니야 ===

--- word ---

type: Pronoun + Particle
breakdown: 나 + -가
meaning: I (as the subject)

--- word ---

type: Verb Clause Modifier
breakdown: 먹다 + -었- + -다는
meaning: that (I) ate
notes: This is a quoting form that modifies a noun. It's a contraction of -다고 하는. It turns the clause 'I ate' (먹었다) into a descriptive phrase that can modify a noun like 것 ('thing' or 'fact').

type: Bound Noun + Particle
breakdown: 것 + 이
meaning: the thing/fact that
notes: A very common colloquial contraction of 것이. 것 is a bound noun meaning 'thing' or 'fact', and -이 is the subject particle. So, 먹었다는 게 means 'the fact that I ate'.

breakdown: 아니다 + -야
meaning: is not
notes: Repeated for emphasis. The full structure 'A는 게 아니다' means 'It's not that A...' or 'It's not the case that A...'. It's a standard way to deny a proposition or clarify a misunderstanding.
--- grammar ---
pattern: Clause + -다는 것 / -다는 게
meaning: A grammar pattern used to nominalize a preceding clause, turning it into a noun phrase meaning 'the fact that...'. It allows an entire sentence-like idea to function as the subject or object of another verb.
example: 그가 온다는 게 사실이야? (Is the fact that he's coming true?)

--- word ---
term: 어쩌겠어?
type: Verb
breakdown: 어쩌다 (to do what/how) + -겠- (conjecture) + -어(요)? (question)
meaning: what can one do?
notes: This is a rhetorical question. The `-겠-` suffix here doesn't indicate the future, but rather expresses a logical conclusion or a lack of other options. The meaning is close to 'What else could I do?' or 'It can't be helped'.

meaning: Used in questions to express doubt, supposition, or a rhetorical point, rather than a simple future action. Often translates to 'I wonder...' or implies there's no other choice.

=== [1:05:11] 얼마야? ===

=== [1:06:19] 이렇게 바르면 ===

notes: An adverb formed from the descriptive verb 이렇다 (to be like this). The -게 suffix is a common way to turn descriptive verbs (adjectives) into adverbs. For example, 예쁘다 (to be pretty) becomes 예쁘게 (prettily).

notes: This is a shortened form of 써야 하다 or 써야 되다, which means 'must use' or 'have to use'. In casual speech, the final 하다/되다 is often omitted when the meaning is clear from context.
--- word ---
term: 하는
type: Verb
breakdown: 하다 + -는
meaning: that (I) do
notes: This is part of the grammar pattern '-어야 하는 것' (a thing one must do). It modifies the noun '것들' (things).
--- word ---
term: 것들
type: Noun
breakdown: 것 + -들
meaning: things
notes: 것 means 'thing'. The suffix -들 is the plural marker in Korean. While not always necessary, it's used here to emphasize that she's talking about multiple items.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V + -아/어야 하다/되다
meaning: Expresses obligation or necessity, meaning 'must' or 'have to'.
example: 숙제를 해야 해요. (I have to do my homework.)

meaning: time, when

breakdown:

--- grammar ---

meaning: Indicates the time when an action or state occurs. Translates to 'when...' or 'at the time of...'.

term: 나는
type: Pronoun + Particle
breakdown: 나 + -는
meaning: as for me / I
notes: '나' is the informal pronoun for 'I', used with friends or people younger than you (반말 - banmal). '-는' is the topic marking particle, indicating that the speaker is talking about themself as the main subject of the sentence.

term: 이제
type: Adverb
breakdown: 
meaning: now

--- grammar ---
pattern: Verb + -는 것
meaning: This pattern, called nominalization, turns a verb phrase into a noun phrase. It's equivalent to 'the act of doing X' or 'the thing that does X'.

breakdown: 되다 -> 되어 -> 돼
meaning: must, have to
notes: The informal conjugation of '되다' (to become, to be okay). '돼' is a contraction of '되어'. When combined with '-아야/어야', it forms the expression of necessity 'must do'.
--- grammar ---
pattern: V-아야/어야 되다/하다
meaning: Expresses obligation or necessity, equivalent to 'must' or 'have to' in English. '되다' and '하다' are largely interchangeable in this pattern, with '되다' sometimes feeling slightly softer.
example: 숙제를 해야 돼. (I have to do my homework.)

example: 밥을 먹고 영화를 봤어요. (I ate and then watched a movie.)
level: Beginner

type: Interjection
breakdown: 
meaning: Bye
notes: Used again as a final sign-off before ending the live stream. Its repetition makes the farewell feel softer and more drawn out, which is common in casual conversations.

=== [1:09:17] 사랑한다 ===
meaning: I love you.
tone: Affectionate, declarative.
--- word ---
term: 사랑한다
type: Verb
breakdown: 사랑하다 + -ㄴ다
meaning: I love you
notes: This is the plain form (or narrative form) of 사랑하다 (to love). While often used in writing (books, diaries), it can be used in speech to make a sincere, almost dramatic declaration. Idols frequently use this form to express their love for their fans as a group. It feels more declarative and impactful than the standard informal 사랑해.

=== [1:09:19] 멍청이들아 ===
meaning: My Twits.
tone: Affectionate, playful, addressing her fans.
--- word ---
term: 멍청이들아
type: Noun + Plural Marker + Vocative Particle
breakdown: 멍청이 + -들 + -아
meaning: Hey Twits / My Twits
notes: 멍청이 means 'idiot' or 'twit', but Hwasa uses it as an affectionate nickname for her fans. -들 is the plural marker. -아 is the informal vocative particle used to call someone whose name ends in a consonant. Using this term of endearment shows the very close and playful relationship she has with her fanbase.

=== [1:09:21] 안녕 ===
meaning: Hi.
tone: Informal, greeting.
--- word ---
term: 안녕
type: Interjection
breakdown: 
meaning: Hi / Hello
notes: A common informal greeting (반말 - banmal) used with friends, people of the same age, or those younger. It can also mean 'Bye' depending on the context. The formal version is 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo). Using '안녕' in a situation that requires formal speech would be considered rude.
